channel.title: Oddly Wired
channel.description: One checked psychology fact a day. Every claim names the study behind it.

item.title: You view strangers as more similar than they are.
item.description: Outgroup homogeneity is the tendency to perceive members of other groups as uniform.

item.title: Doing a favor for someone makes you like them.
item.description: The Ben Franklin effect demonstrates that helping someone actually increases your affection for them.

item.title: You overestimate how your future self will feel.
item.description: The projection bias causes you to project your current tastes or preferences onto your future decisions.

item.title: You falsely believe you predicted the outcome.
item.description: Hindsight bias causes you to view events as inevitable after they have occurred.

item.title: You assume attractive people possess other positive traits.
item.description: The halo effect causes people to perceive physically appealing individuals as more intelligent and honest.

item.title: You value an object more because you own it.
item.description: The endowment effect describes a persistent discrepancy between willingness-to-accept (WTA) and willingness-to-pay (WTP) valuations observed in experiments.

item.title: You believe you are more unique than you are.
item.description: The false uniqueness effect leads you to overestimate how rare your own positive traits and abilities actually are.

item.title: You judge your actions by intent but others by outcomes.
item.description: The actor-observer hypothesis, proposed by Jones and Nisbett in 1971, posits that individuals attribute their own actions to situational factors and others' actions to dispositional ones, though this effect has not held up in comprehensive meta-analyses.

item.title: You think your personal memories are objectively accurate.
item.description: Source monitoring errors lead you to misattribute the origin of your memories.

item.title: You stop helping the moment a witness appears.
item.description: The bystander effect shows that the presence of other people decreases your likelihood of acting in an emergency.

item.title: You think your happiness depends on one specific circumstance.
item.description: Focalism is the tendency to overestimate the extent to which one specific event will impact your long-term emotional state.

item.title: You prefer being accurately judged over being falsely praised.
item.description: Self-verification theory suggests that people seek feedback that confirms their own existing self-concept.

item.title: You want what you are told you cannot have.
item.description: Psychological reactance is a motivational state that occurs when your freedom to choose is threatened or eliminated.

item.title: You claim success for a team you barely know.
item.description: Basking in reflected glory (BIRGing) is the tendency to align with successful groups to bolster self-esteem or social image, while cutting off reflected failure (CORFing) is the separate tendency to distance oneself from failing groups.

item.title: You feel more attraction when your heart rate is high.
item.description: The misattribution of arousal causes you to interpret unrelated physical excitement as romantic interest.

item.title: You change your own behavior when being watched.
item.description: The 'Hawthorne effect' is a popular but scientifically contested term used to describe the hypothesis that subjects change their behavior due to being observed, although the original 1920s studies are often cited as evidence despite methodological flaws.

item.title: People perform better because you expect them to.
item.description: Higher performance expectations lead to improved outcomes for the individuals being observed.

item.title: You will always underestimate the time a task takes.
item.description: People consistently predict they will complete tasks faster than they actually do.

item.title: You believe bad things only happen to others.
item.description: You consistently underestimate the probability that you will experience negative life events.

item.title: Your brain is programmed to ignore the middle.
item.description: The serial position effect was first identified and described by Hermann Ebbinghaus in 1885.

item.title: Losing ten dollars feels worse than winning ten feels.
item.description: Kahneman and Tversky's 1992 paper established that the pain of losing is approximately 2.25 times more powerful than the joy of gaining.

item.title: You are constantly filtering conversations you are not hearing.
item.description: A 1953 study by Colin Cherry established the cocktail party problem, demonstrating the brain's strong tendency to filter out unattended audio streams.

item.title: You remember information better when it relates to yourself.
item.description: A 1977 study found that words are recalled far more accurately if they are processed in relation to one's own traits.

item.title: You cannot accurately predict your own emotional responses.
item.description: A 2005 study showed that people in a calm state consistently underestimate how much intense emotions will drive their behavior.

item.title: You like things more simply because you saw them.
item.description: A 1968 study demonstrated that participants rated nonsense symbols as more positive after repeated, brief exposures.

item.title: You filter reality to fit what you already know.
item.description: Humans systematically favor information that confirms their existing beliefs.

item.title: You can remember events that never actually happened.
item.description: Leading questions can bias eyewitness testimony and retrospectively influence how events are reported.

item.title: You choose the middle option to avoid extremes.
item.description: A third, inferior option can make the other choices more attractive.

item.title: You perform better at simple tasks when others watch.
item.description: The presence of an audience increases your speed on easy tasks.

item.title: You feel less guilty when you choose inaction.
item.description: Humans assign more moral weight to active harm than passive neglect.

item.title: You gauge risk by the news, not logic.
item.description: You estimate the probability of events based on how easily examples arise.

item.title: You think you knew the outcome all along.
item.description: Your memory of your past confidence changes once you learn the truth.

item.title: You assume your private opinions are the majority view.
item.description: You consistently overestimate how much others agree with your personal beliefs.

item.title: Your brain ignores uniform items but highlights the oddity.
item.description: The Von Restorff effect states that an item that stands out from a group of similar items is more likely to be remembered.

item.title: You judge your current life against those performing better.
item.description: The term 'upward social comparison' emerged from later developments in social comparison theory, building upon but distinct from Festinger's original 1954 work.

item.title: You reach different conclusions depending on how options are presented.
item.description: The framing effect describes how your decision-making shifts based on whether an outcome is described in terms of gains or losses.

item.title: Your personal effort drops when you join a group.
item.description: The phenomenon of decreased group effort is often termed 'social loafing,' a term coined by Latané et al. in 1979, which is historically rooted in the 'Ringelmann effect' documented in 1913.

item.title: You ignore the length of an experience in your memory.
item.description: Duration neglect is a heuristic where the duration of an experience is assigned little weight relative to the emotional 'peak' and 'end' of the event when forming a retrospective evaluation.

item.title: You are blind to the reasons for your own choices.
item.description: Choice blindness is the phenomenon where people fail to notice when their own decisions are manipulated, yet they readily invent reasons for the outcome.

item.title: A final sound can wipe out your last memory.
item.description: The suffix effect is the finding that recall of the final items in a list is inhibited if an irrelevant, spoken sound is presented immediately after the list ends.

item.title: Your feelings dictate your risk assessment before logic starts.
item.description: The affect heuristic is the process of using current emotions to make rapid decisions instead of evaluating complex data.

item.title: You find personal meaning in descriptions written for everyone.
item.description: The Barnum effect is the psychological phenomenon where individuals believe that vague, generic personality descriptions apply specifically to them.

item.title: You naturally remember yourself doing more work than others.
item.description: The egocentric bias leads individuals to claim more responsibility for a collective outcome than they objectively contributed.

item.title: You lose the ability to teach once you learn.
item.description: The curse of knowledge describes the inability to imagine that other people do not know what you know.

item.title: Your mind is trapped by the first number you hear.
item.description: The anchoring effect causes individuals to rely too heavily on the initial piece of information offered when making subsequent judgments.

item.title: You judge the actions of your group more leniently.
item.description: When a member of your own group fails, you attribute it to bad luck; when an outsider fails, you attribute it to their incompetence.

item.title: You are functionally blind for half a second.
item.description: The attentional blink is a performance deficit where individuals struggle to identify a second target in a rapid sequence of stimuli when it appears within 200-500ms of a first target.

item.title: You retain information better when you create it yourself.
item.description: Information generated through your own effort is remembered better than information read or heard passively.

item.title: Simply predicting your behavior makes you more likely to act.
item.description: When people are asked to predict whether they will perform a behavior, they are statistically more likely to perform that behavior later.

item.title: You believe you influenced an outcome that was random.
item.description: When individuals are given a choice in a game of chance, they rate their probability of success as higher than those who were assigned an outcome.
